title: State machines and logic families
subtitle: Turn a behaviour described in words into states, a transition table and finally flip-flops and gates — then meet the silicon it runs on.

fsm.title: Finite state machines
fsm.body: A finite state machine has a set of states, inputs, a next-state rule and outputs. In a Moore machine the output depends only on the state; in a Mealy machine on state and input (so it can react a clock earlier and may need fewer states). A state diagram draws states as circles and transitions as labelled arrows.

seq.title: A sequence detector
seq.body: Design a detector that raises its output when the input ends in 11. States: q0 (no progress), q1 (last bit was a 1), q2 (saw 11). On input 1 move forward (q0→q1→q2, and q2 stays); on input 0 fall back to q0. The machine accepts yes for 0110111 (final q2) and no for 0101 (final q1).

design.title: From diagram to circuit
design.body: 1) Draw the state diagram. 2) Assign binary codes to states (n flip-flops for up to 2ⁿ states). 3) Write the state table: present state, input → next state, output. 4) Use each flip-flop’s excitation table to get input equations; simplify them with K-maps. 5) Draw the circuit and check unused states go somewhere safe.
design.steps: A machine has 5 states. Flip-flops needed: 2² = 4 < 5 ≤ 8 = 2³.

ttl.title: Logic families and their numbers
ttl.body: Gates are built in families. TTL (bipolar, 5 V) is fast but power-hungry; CMOS (complementary MOSFETs) uses almost no power except when switching and is the basis of all modern chips. Key figures: propagation delay (how long an output takes to change), power dissipation, noise margin (NM = VIH − VOH style gap between output and input thresholds) and fan-out (how many inputs one output can drive).
ttl.steps: A gate outputs at least 4.0 V for a 1 and the next gate accepts any input ≥ 3.5 V as 1. High-level noise margin = V_OH(min) − V_IH(min).

cmos.title: CMOS inverter and NAND
cmos.body: A CMOS inverter is a PMOS (pull-up to VDD) over an NMOS (pull-down to ground) sharing gate and output: input 0 turns the PMOS on, output 1; input 1 turns the NMOS on, output 0. Only one conducts in steady state, so static power is near zero; power is spent charging and discharging load capacitance: P = C·V²·f. A NAND puts two NMOS in series and two PMOS in parallel.
cmos.steps: C = 10 pF, V = 3.3 V, f = 50 MHz. Dynamic power P = C V² f.

mem.title: Programmable logic and memory
mem.body: Instead of wiring gates, load a configuration: a ROM is a look-up table (2ⁿ words of m bits implement any m functions of n inputs); a PLA/PAL programs AND and OR planes; an FPGA has thousands of small look-up tables and flip-flops joined by programmable routing. Memory: SRAM (flip-flop cell, fast, 6 transistors) vs DRAM (capacitor, dense, refreshed).
mem.steps: A 4-input look-up table stores one output bit for each input pattern. Number of bits stored: 2⁴.
